newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ poised for stern monetary management after CPI.
newsitem.headline: NZ poised for stern monetary management after CPI.

text.p: New Zealand financial markets were ready for a tough line from the Reserve Bank on Tuesday after inflation data dashed their high hopes, even though the figures were in line with a clear consensus of expectations.

The New Zealand dollar had weakened ahead of the data, easing monetary conditions below a level outlined as desired by the central bank, as dealers second-guessed an inflation figure lower than forecasts.
"Market conditions are too easy and the market is playing a dangerous game if it's going to continue (to trade rates) outside the bank's comfort zone," said First NZ Capital economist Jason Wong.
"They have given two warnings already, that obviously hasn't been enough, so you are looking at a change in the settlement cash target (as a response)."
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand calculated that underlying inflation rose by 0.3 percent in the June quarter, for an annual rate of 1.49 percent.
Earlier, Statistics NZ said consumer price inflation rose 0.1 percent in the quarter for an annual rate of 1.1 percent, one of the lowest rates in the OECD.
All the figures were in line with market economists' expectations as well as the Reserve Bank's own recent forecasts.

Amid a frenzied build-up to today's data, when currency traders discounted a lower-than-expected result and pushed down the value of the kiwi dollar, the RB on Friday issued its second warning in eight days that market conditions were too easy.
Just before today's data release conditions, as measured by the bank's Monetary Conditions Index (MCI) were actually looser than they had been on Friday.
However, the index later adjusted from 753 to 770, some 55 basis points in interest rate terms easier than the RB has identified as desirable and close to its 50 b.p. comfort range.
The adjustment mainly came via the New Zealand dollar which rose to 66.75 U.S. cents from 66.63 before the inflation data.
The MCI combines the dollar and 90-day bank bill interest rates.
Bankers Trust New Zealand chief economist David Plank said the markets' disappointment masked an otherwise good result.
"It's an excellent number that puts inflation at the mid-point of the Reserve Bank's (0-3 percent target) band.
"It means the trend towards lower inflation is firmly established (and) annual inflation will continue to fall for the rest of this year."

The dilemma for the RB is that if the markets continue to ignore it and it is forced to tighten by lowering the cash target (the amount of cash overnight in the banking system) it would be doing so while the economy is in a fragile state.
GDP fell in the March quarter by 0.5 percent and while RB Governor Don Brash has said activity picked up in the June quarter, there is scant evidence of rising confidence.
Prime Minister Jim Bolger told a farmers' meeting he had sympathy with their frustration at the RB keeping things tight.
"Many of you will have greeted the Reserve Bank's cautionary statement last Friday with some exasperation. I have to say I have some sympathy with you," he said.

He said the strength of the kiwi dollar had made exporting hard and many would see last week's news that the current account deficit was at 4.8 percent of GDP as vindication of farmers' warnings of the impact of the high dollar.
"Like you it is with some relief that I see signs that the very tough monetary conditions we have had to experience of late may be able to be relaxed a little," Bolger said.
